title: Mask R-CNN
description: Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN by adding a parallel mask prediction branch and RoI Align, enabling accurate instance segmentation on top of object detection.

body.raw: ## Context and Motivation Faster R-CNN was a major step forward because it combined region proposals and classification into one deep learning framework. But despite its accuracy, it had a clear limitation: it could only draw bounding boxes around objects. A bounding box is useful, but it is a very rough way to represent object shape. Think about a person riding a bicycle. The bounding box will cover both the rider and the bike, but it does not tell us which pixels belong to the person and which belong to the bike. In many applications, this coarse representation is not enough. Self-driving cars, for example, need to know the exact shape of pedestrians and other vehicles for safe navigation. In medical imaging, it is important to mark the precise region of a tumor, not just a rectangle around it. This is where segmentation comes in. Instead of just detecting objects, segmentation aims to label each pixel. Semantic segmentation does this at the category level, but it cannot separate multiple instances of the same class. What we really need is **instance segmentation**: identifying each object and outlining its pixels individually. Mask R-CNN was introduced to solve exactly this problem. The idea was to take the strong two stage framework of Faster R-CNN and extend it by adding a branch that predicts masks for each region of interest. At the same time, the authors addressed a key weakness of Faster R-CNN: the small misalignments caused by RoI Pooling. They introduced RoI Align, a simple but crucial change that made pixel-level mask predictions possible. The result was a model that could not only detect objects and refine bounding boxes, but also predict accurate binary masks for every object in an image. ## Architecture Breakdown Mask R-CNN builds directly on Faster R-CNN, but with some important upgrades that allow it to predict accurate masks. The overall flow is still two stage: first generate proposals, then classify them and predict masks. Let us walk through the steps in detail. ### Step 1: Backbone CNN with Feature Pyramid Network Mask R-CNN uses ResNet as its backbone, but with an important addition: the Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). The idea of the FPN is to create multi-scale feature maps so that both small and large objects can be represented effectively. Without the FPN, deep layers of the backbone lose too much spatial resolution, which makes detecting small objects difficult. #### How ResNet alone works Suppose we input an 800 × 800 image into ResNet-50. After each stage of convolution and pooling, the spatial size shrinks while the number of channels grows: - After conv2 → 200 × 200 × 256 feature map (stride 4). - After conv3 → 100 × 100 × 512 feature map (stride 8). - After conv4 → 50 × 50 × 1024 feature map (stride 16). - After conv5 → 25 × 25 × 2048 feature map (stride 32). Now imagine there is a 32 × 32 object in the input image. At stride 32, this object shrinks to 32 ÷ 32 = 1 pixel. That is not enough detail to localize it. On the other hand, the shallow conv2 layer has fine detail, but weaker semantic features. This mismatch is exactly what the FPN solves. #### How FPN is built The FPN introduces a **top-down pathway with lateral connections**. The idea is to combine the strong semantics of deep layers with the fine resolution of shallow layers. Here is the step-by-step construction: 1. Start with conv5 (25 × 25 × 2048). Use a 1 × 1 convolution to reduce it to 256 channels. This becomes **P5**. 2. Upsample P5 by a factor of 2 (25 × 25 → 50 × 50). Add it elementwise to conv4, which is also reduced to 256 channels with a 1 × 1 convolution. This forms **P4**: $P_4 = W_1 \cdot C_4 + \text{Upsample}(P_5)$ 3. Repeat the process: upsample P4 (50 × 50 → 100 × 100) and add it to conv3 (after 1 × 1 conv). This forms **P3**. 4. Again: upsample P3 (100 × 100 → 200 × 200) and add it to conv2 (after 1 × 1 conv). This forms **P2**. Each Pi is passed through a 3 × 3 convolution to clean up aliasing artifacts. The final pyramid has consistent 256 channel feature maps: - P2 → 200 × 200 × 256 - P3 → 100 × 100 × 256 - P4 → 50 × 50 × 256 - P5 → 25 × 25 × 256 #### Assigning regions to pyramid levels Once the pyramid is built, the model decides which feature map to use for each region. The level is chosen based on the size of the region using the formula: $k = \lfloor k_0 + \log_2 \left( \frac{\sqrt{wh}}{224} \right) \rfloor$ where $w$ and $h$ are the width and height of the region, and $k_0 = 4$ (reference to P4). Examples: - A 32 × 32 region → $\sqrt{wh} = 32$. Plugging in gives $k = 2$. Use **P2**. - A 224 × 224 region → $\sqrt{wh} = 224$. Plugging in gives $k = 4$. Use **P4**. - A 512 × 512 region → $\sqrt{wh} = 512$. Plugging in gives $k = 5$. Use **P5**. #### Why this matters The FPN makes it possible to detect objects of all scales with one unified backbone. Small objects are processed at higher resolution maps, while large objects use coarser maps with stronger semantics. The important thing to note is that the FPN is still part of the **backbone**. It does not generate proposals — that job still belongs to the RPN, which we will cover in Step 2. ### Step 2: Region Proposal Network The Region Proposal Network in Mask R-CNN works the same way as in Faster R-CNN: a small 3 × 3 sliding window scans over the feature map, and for each spatial location it predicts a set of anchors. Each anchor is scored with an objectness score (object vs background) and refined with bounding box deltas. What changes in Mask R-CNN is that the RPN now operates on **all levels of the FPN pyramid**. For example, consider the feature maps we just built: - P2 → 200 × 200 (stride 4) - P3 → 100 × 100 (stride 8) - P4 → 50 × 50 (stride 16) - P5 → 25 × 25 (stride 32) Anchors are generated at every location in each map. Suppose we use 3 scales and 3 aspect ratios. That means 9 anchors per location. On P2, with 200 × 200 locations, that is 360,000 anchors. On P3, with 100 × 100, it is 90,000 anchors, and so on. Across all pyramid levels, the RPN easily handles half a million anchors in one image. This might sound expensive, but the convolutional operations are shared, so the cost is manageable. After scoring and refining, proposals from all pyramid levels are merged. Non Maximum Suppression is then applied to filter redundant boxes, and the top 1000 to 2000 proposals are selected for the next stage. The advantage of this design is clear: - Small objects are proposed from high-resolution maps like P2. - Large objects are proposed from coarse maps like P5. By tying the RPN to the pyramid, Mask R-CNN inherits the multi-scale power of FPN while keeping the same efficient proposal mechanism as Faster R-CNN. ### Step 3: RoI Align One of the key contributions of Mask R-CNN is **RoI Align**, which fixes the spatial misalignment introduced by RoI Pooling. To understand why it is important, let us carefully walk through the difference. #### The problem with RoI Pooling Suppose the RPN proposes a region of interest on the feature map with floating point coordinates: (15.2, 23.7, 47.8, 68.3). These numbers represent the top-left and bottom-right corners of the proposal on the feature map. In **RoI Pooling**, these values are rounded to integers: (15, 24, 48, 68). The region is then divided into a fixed grid, say 7 × 7, and max pooling is applied in each bin. The issue is that rounding shifts the boundaries. A pixel shift of even 0.5 in the feature map corresponds to a 16-pixel shift in the input image when the stride is 32. For masks, this tiny shift can mean that object boundaries no longer line up correctly. #### How RoI Align fixes it RoI Align removes rounding and uses **bilinear interpolation** instead of max pooling. Let us work through an example. Take the same RoI: (15.2, 23.7, 47.8, 68.3). We want to pool it into a 2 × 2 grid (to keep the math simple; in practice it is usually 7 × 7). 1. Divide the RoI into bins: - Width = 47.8 – 15.2 = 32.6 - Height = 68.3 – 23.7 = 44.6 - Each bin is therefore 16.3 × 22.3 in size. 2. For each bin, select four sampling points at evenly spaced fractional coordinates. Example: the top-left bin might include points like (16.1, 25.9), (24.2, 25.9), (16.1, 36.3), (24.2, 36.3). 3. Compute the feature value at each fractional coordinate using bilinear interpolation. Suppose (24.2, 25.9) lies between four neighboring pixels with values v1, v2, v3, v4. Then: $V(x, y) = \sum_{i=1}^{4} w_i \cdot v_i$ where the weights $w_i$ are proportional to the distances from (x, y) to each pixel center. 4. Take the average of the four sampled values to get the output for that bin. Repeating this for all bins gives a perfectly aligned 2 × 2 feature map (or 7 × 7 in practice). No rounding, no quantization, just smooth interpolation. #### Why it matters For bounding boxes, the difference between RoI Pooling and RoI Align is small. But for masks, pixel accuracy is critical. Without RoI Align, masks often look jagged and misaligned with the object edges. With RoI Align, the masks line up smoothly with boundaries, which was essential for the success of Mask R-CNN. #### Visual reference The original Mask R-CNN paper has a simple and clear figure comparing RoI Pooling and RoI Align: [Figure 3 in the paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.06870.pdf) shows how quantization misaligns features and how RoI Align fixes it. ### Step 4: Detection Head Once RoI Align has converted each proposal into a fixed-size feature map, these features are fed into the detection head. The detection head is responsible for two tasks: predicting the class of the object and refining the bounding box coordinates. This part of the architecture is essentially the same as in Faster R-CNN. #### Input and shape Suppose the backbone is ResNet with FPN and we pool each proposal into a 7 × 7 grid. If the FPN outputs 256 channels, then each RoI after RoI Align has shape 256 × 7 × 7. Flattening this gives 12,544 features per RoI. #### Fully connected layers These features are passed through two fully connected layers (often with 1024 or 4096 hidden units). The network learns abstract, high-level representations of the region that are useful for classification and box regression. $\text{RoI feature} \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 7 \times 7}$ $\;\;\rightarrow\;\; \mathbb{R}^{12544}$ $\;\;\rightarrow\;\; \mathbb{R}^{1024}$ $\;\;\rightarrow\;\; \mathbb{R}^{1024}$ #### Classification branch One branch of the detection head outputs class scores. If there are K object categories, the classifier outputs K + 1 probabilities (the +1 is for the background class). For example, if there are 80 classes as in COCO, the classifier outputs an 81-dimensional vector for each RoI. The highest probability decides the predicted class. #### Bounding box regression branch The second branch outputs bounding box adjustments. For each class, it predicts four values: $\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta w, \Delta h$. These represent how to shift and resize the RoI to better fit the object. In COCO with 80 classes, this branch outputs 80 × 4 = 320 numbers per RoI. At inference time, only the regression for the predicted class is used to refine the bounding box. #### Why keep it this way? The detection head in Mask R-CNN is deliberately left unchanged from Faster R-CNN. The logic is simple: Faster R-CNN already gave state-of-the-art results for detection. Instead of reinventing this part, the authors extended it by adding a **third branch** for masks, which we will cover in the next step. This modular design made it possible for Mask R-CNN to inherit the strong detection performance of Faster R-CNN while extending it to segmentation. ### Step 5: Mask Head The main innovation of Mask R-CNN is the addition of a **mask prediction branch**. This branch runs in parallel with the detection head and produces a pixel-level binary mask for each object. While the detection head only outputs class scores and bounding box refinements, the mask head predicts a much finer representation: the outline of the object itself. #### Input and shape After RoI Align, each proposal has a feature map of size 256 × 14 × 14 (the paper increased the resolution from 7 × 7 in Faster R-CNN to 14 × 14 for more spatial detail). These features are fed into the mask head. #### Network structure The mask head is a small Fully Convolutional Network (FCN). Instead of fully connected layers, it uses convolutional layers so that spatial information is preserved. A typical structure is: - 4 convolutional layers, each 3 × 3 with 256 filters. - 1 deconvolution (transpose convolution) layer that upsamples by 2×. - 1 final 1 × 1 convolution layer to output masks. #### Output dimensions If there are K classes, the mask head outputs K binary masks for each RoI. Each mask is 28 × 28 pixels in size. For example, in COCO with 80 classes, the output per RoI is 80 × 28 × 28. At inference time, only the mask corresponding to the predicted class (from the detection head) is kept. For example, if the detection head predicts “person” for a proposal, we take only the “person” mask from the 80 outputs. #### Training the mask head The mask branch is trained with a per-pixel **binary cross entropy loss**. For each positive RoI, the ground truth mask is cropped to the RoI and resized to 28 × 28. Only the mask for the true class is used in the loss — this prevents competition between classes and makes training more stable. #### Why this works By separating the mask prediction into its own branch, Mask R-CNN keeps the detection head focused on classification and bounding box refinement, while the mask head specializes in pixel-level segmentation. This parallel design is efficient because both branches share the same RoI features from RoI Align. The 28 × 28 mask is coarse compared to the original image, but it can be upsampled later to the input resolution. Even at this size, it is accurate enough to capture fine object boundaries. #### Visual reference The architecture of the mask head is shown clearly in the original Mask R-CNN paper: [Figure 2 in the paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.06870.pdf) illustrates the three parallel branches — classification, bounding box regression, and mask prediction. ## Training Procedure Training Mask R-CNN is more involved than Faster R-CNN because it now has three main objectives: classification, bounding box regression, and mask prediction. The key idea is to optimize all of them together with a multi-task loss. #### Step 1: RPN loss The Region Proposal Network is trained the same way as in Faster R-CNN. At each anchor, the RPN predicts whether the anchor is foreground (contains an object) or background. The classification loss is a binary cross entropy, and the regression loss adjusts anchor coordinates with a smooth L1 loss. $ L_{\text{RPN}} = L_{\text{cls}}^{\text{RPN}} + L_{\text{reg}}^{\text{RPN}} $ where - $L_{\text{cls}}^{\text{RPN}} = - \big[ y \log p + (1-y)\log(1-p) \big]$ - $L_{\text{reg}}^{\text{RPN}} = \text{smooth}_{L1}(t - t^*)$ Here $y \in \{0,1\}$ is the ground truth label, $p$ is the predicted probability, $t$ are the predicted box offsets, and $t^*$ are the ground truth offsets. #### Step 2: Detection head loss The detection head also has two branches. The classification branch predicts a distribution over K + 1 categories (K object classes plus background). The loss here is a softmax cross entropy: $ L_{\text{cls}}^{\text{det}} = - \sum_{c=1}^{K+1} y_c \log p_c $ where $y_c$ is the ground truth one-hot vector and $p_c$ are the predicted probabilities. The bounding box regression branch predicts 4 values per class: $\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta w, \Delta h$. Only the regression for the true class is used in the loss, again with smooth L1: $ L_{\text{reg}}^{\text{det}} = \text{smooth}_{L1}(t - t^*) $ #### Step 3: Mask loss The mask branch predicts a binary mask for each class. Suppose the RoI is assigned to class $k$. Then only the kth mask is used in the loss, while the others are ignored. This prevents the mask head from wasting capacity on irrelevant classes. The loss is a pixel-wise binary cross entropy averaged over all pixels in the 28 × 28 mask: $ L_{\text{mask}} = - \frac{1}{m^2} \sum_{i,j} \big[ y_{ij}\log \hat{y}_{ij} + (1-y_{ij})\log (1-\hat{y}_{ij}) \big] $ where $m = 28$, $y_{ij}$ is the ground truth mask value at pixel (i,j), and $\hat{y}_{ij}$ is the predicted probability. #### Step 4: Final loss The total loss is simply the sum of all the components: $ L = L_{\text{RPN}} + L_{\text{cls}}^{\text{det}} + L_{\text{reg}}^{\text{det}} + L_{\text{mask}} $ This allows the backbone, RPN, detection head, and mask head to be trained end-to-end in one framework. Gradients flow through all branches, and the shared backbone features are updated in a way that benefits every task. #### Training details - **Mini-batches**: Typically 256 RoIs per image are sampled for the detection head, balanced between positive and negative samples. - **Mask targets**: Ground truth masks are cropped to the RoI and resized to 28 × 28. - **Backbone initialization**: ResNet is usually pretrained on ImageNet before being fine-tuned within Mask R-CNN. - **Optimization**: SGD with momentum is used, often with learning rate schedules like step decay. By training all tasks jointly, Mask R-CNN learns representations that are useful for detection and segmentation at the same time, without the need for separate networks. ## Implementation Notes Let us now translate Mask R-CNN into practical steps. We will write down the code structure as if we were implementing the model from scratch in PyTorch. This helps connect the theory to actual practice. We start with the backbone and the Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). ### Step 1: Backbone CNN with Feature Pyramid Network Mask R-CNN uses ResNet as the backbone, often ResNet-50 or ResNet-101. To build an FPN on top of it, we need to extract feature maps at different stages of the ResNet. These are usually taken from conv2, conv3, conv4, and conv5. Their strides are 4, 8, 16, and 32 relative to the input image. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn import torchvision.models as models class ResNetBackbone(nn.Module): def __init__(self, name="resnet50"): super().__init__() # Load pretrained ResNet resnet = getattr(models, name)(pretrained=True) # Keep only the convolutional layers, discard final avgpool + fc # ResNet is structured as: stem -> layer1 -> layer2 -> layer3 -> layer4 self.stem = nn.Sequential( resnet.conv1, # 7x7 conv resnet.bn1, resnet.relu, resnet.maxpool ) self.layer1 = resnet.layer1 # conv2, stride 4 self.layer2 = resnet.layer2 # conv3, stride 8 self.layer3 = resnet.layer3 # conv4, stride 16 self.layer4 = resnet.layer4 # conv5, stride 32 def forward(self, x): c1 = self.stem(x) # stride 4 c2 = self.layer1(c1) # stride 4 (conv2) c3 = self.layer2(c2) # stride 8 (conv3) c4 = self.layer3(c3) # stride 16 (conv4) c5 = self.layer4(c4) # stride 32 (conv5) return c2, c3, c4, c5 ``` At this point, for an 800 × 800 input image: - c2 has shape [B, 256, 200, 200] - c3 has shape [B, 512, 100, 100] - c4 has shape [B, 1024, 50, 50] - c5 has shape [B, 2048, 25, 25] ### Building the FPN layers We now build the top-down pathway with lateral connections. The idea is to reduce each feature map to 256 channels with a 1×1 convolution, then progressively upsample and add to the next shallower map. ```python class FPN(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels_list, out_channels=256): """ in_channels_list: [256, 512, 1024, 2048] from ResNet stages out_channels: usually 256 """ super().__init__() # 1x1 conv layers for lateral connections self.lateral_convs = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Conv2d(in_ch, out_channels, kernel_size=1) for in_ch in in_channels_list ]) # 3x3 conv layers to smooth after merging self.output_convs = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1) for _ in in_channels_list ]) def forward(self, inputs): # inputs: [c2, c3, c4, c5] c2, c3, c4, c5 = inputs # Step 1: reduce c5 to 256 channels p5 = self.lateral_convs[3](c5) # Step 2: build P4 by upsampling P5 and adding to c4 p4 = self.lateral_convs[2](c4) + nn.functional.interpolate( p5, size=c4.shape[-2:], mode="nearest" ) # Step 3: build P3 p3 = self.lateral_convs[1](c3) + nn.functional.interpolate( p4, size=c3.shape[-2:], mode="nearest" ) # Step 4: build P2 p2 = self.lateral_convs[0](c2) + nn.functional.interpolate( p3, size=c2.shape[-2:], mode="nearest" ) # Final 3x3 conv to smooth p5 = self.output_convs[3](p5) p4 = self.output_convs[2](p4) p3 = self.output_convs[1](p3) p2 = self.output_convs[0](p2) return p2, p3, p4, p5 ``` ### Checking the shapes If the input image is 800 × 800, the output pyramid maps are: - P2 → [B, 256, 200, 200] - P3 → [B, 256, 100, 100] - P4 → [B, 256, 50, 50] - P5 → [B, 256, 25, 25] All of them have the same depth (256 channels) but different resolutions. These maps are now ready to be used by the RPN in the next step. Example usage: ```python backbone = ResNetBackbone("resnet50") fpn = FPN([256, 512, 1024, 2048], 256) x = torch.randn(1, 3, 800, 800) # batch of 1 image c2, c3, c4, c5 = backbone(x) p2, p3, p4, p5 = fpn([c2, c3, c4, c5]) print(p2.shape, p3.shape, p4.shape, p5.shape) # torch.Size([1, 256, 200, 200]) # torch.Size([1, 256, 100, 100]) # torch.Size([1, 256, 50, 50]) # torch.Size([1, 256, 25, 25]) ``` This matches exactly what we expect from the FPN construction we described earlier. ### Step 2: Region Proposal Network (RPN) The Region Proposal Network is applied on each FPN level (P2, P3, P4, P5). At every location on these maps, the RPN places multiple **anchors** of different scales and aspect ratios. For each anchor, it predicts two things: whether it contains an object (objectness score) and how to refine its coordinates (box regression deltas). ### RPN Head The RPN head is small and fully convolutional. It has three parts: 1. A 3×3 convolution that processes the feature map at each location. 2. A classification layer that predicts foreground vs background for every anchor. 3. A regression layer that predicts four offsets (Δx, Δy, Δw, Δh) for every anchor. ```python class RPNHead(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, num_anchors): super().__init__() self.conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1) self.cls_logits = nn.Conv2d(256, num_anchors * 2, kernel_size=1) self.bbox_pred = nn.Conv2d(256, num_anchors * 4, kernel_size=1) def forward(self, x): # x: [B, 256, H, W] t = nn.functional.relu(self.conv(x)) logits = self.cls_logits(t) # [B, num_anchors*2, H, W] bbox = self.bbox_pred(t) # [B, num_anchors*4, H, W] return logits, bbox ``` If we use 3 scales × 3 aspect ratios = 9 anchors per location, then: - cls_logits outputs 18 channels (9 anchors × 2 classes). - bbox_pred outputs 36 channels (9 anchors × 4 coords). ### Anchor generation For every location in each pyramid map, we generate anchors. Each anchor is centered at the pixel location, with predefined scales and aspect ratios. Let’s write a generator. ```python import itertools import torch def generate_anchors(base_size, scales, ratios, feat_h, feat_w, stride): anchors = [] for y, x in itertools.product(range(feat_h), range(feat_w)): center_x, center_y = x * stride, y * stride for scale in scales: for ratio in ratios: w = scale * (ratio ** 0.5) h = scale / (ratio ** 0.5) anchors.append([ center_x - w / 2, center_y - h / 2, center_x + w / 2, center_y + h / 2 ]) return torch.tensor(anchors) # [N, 4] ``` ### Example: Number of anchors On P3 (stride = 8, feature map size 100 × 100), with 9 anchors per location: $ 100 \times 100 \times 9 = 90{,}000 \; \text{anchors} $ Across all pyramid levels P2–P5, this easily adds up to more than 500,000 anchors per image. ### Bounding box decoding The RPN outputs regression deltas that adjust anchors into refined boxes. Given an anchor $(x_a, y_a, w_a, h_a)$ and predicted deltas $(t_x, t_y, t_w, t_h)$, the refined box is computed as: $ x = x_a + t_x \cdot w_a $ $ y = y_a + t_y \cdot h_a $ $ w = w_a \cdot e^{t_w} $ $ h = h_a \cdot e^{t_h} $ The final box coordinates are then reconstructed from the new center $(x, y)$ and dimensions $(w, h)$. ```python def apply_deltas_to_anchors(anchors, deltas): # anchors: [N, 4], deltas: [N, 4] xa = (anchors[:, 0] + anchors[:, 2]) / 2 ya = (anchors[:, 1] + anchors[:, 3]) / 2 wa = anchors[:, 2] - anchors[:, 0] ha = anchors[:, 3] - anchors[:, 1] tx, ty, tw, th = deltas[:, 0], deltas[:, 1], deltas[:, 2], deltas[:, 3] x = xa + tx * wa y = ya + ty * ha w = wa * torch.exp(tw) h = ha * torch.exp(th) x1 = x - w / 2 y1 = y - h / 2 x2 = x + w / 2 y2 = y + h / 2 return torch.stack([x1, y1, x2, y2], dim=1) ``` ### Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) After generating boxes, many overlap. NMS is applied to keep the top-scoring boxes and remove redundant ones. ```python from torchvision.ops import nms def filter_proposals(boxes, scores, nms_thresh=0.7, top_n=2000): keep = nms(boxes, scores, iou_threshold=nms_thresh) keep = keep[:top_n] # keep top N proposals return boxes[keep], scores[keep] ``` ### Putting it together For each pyramid map P2–P5: - Generate anchors for that map. - Pass the map through the RPN head → get logits and deltas. - Decode deltas into refined boxes. - Apply NMS. - Collect top proposals. The proposals from all pyramid levels are then merged and passed to RoI Align. This completes Step 2. The RPN, when combined with FPN, gives a balanced set of proposals for objects of all sizes - small objects from P2, large objects from P5. ### Step 3: RoI Align RoI Align replaces RoI Pooling to fix spatial misalignment. The key difference is that instead of rounding proposal coordinates to integers, RoI Align uses the exact floating-point values and samples the features with bilinear interpolation. #### The problem with RoI Pooling Suppose the RPN proposes a region of interest with coordinates: $ (x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2) = (15.2, 23.7, 47.8, 68.3) $ RoI Pooling rounds these to integers: $ (15, 24, 48, 68) $ This rounding shifts the region boundaries. With a stride of 32 in the backbone, a 0.5 pixel shift at the feature map level can mean a 16-pixel misalignment in the input image. This is catastrophic for mask prediction, where every pixel matters. #### How RoI Align works Let us say we want to pool this region into a 2 × 2 output (simplified from the usual 7 × 7). 1. The RoI width and height are: $ w = 47.8 - 15.2 = 32.6, \quad h = 68.3 - 23.7 = 44.6 $ Each bin is therefore $w/2 = 16.3$ by $h/2 = 22.3$. 2. In the top-left bin, choose four sampling points at fractional coordinates, for example: $ (16.1, 25.9), (24.2, 25.9), (16.1, 36.3), (24.2, 36.3) $ 3. For each sampling point, compute the feature value with bilinear interpolation. If a point $(x, y)$ falls between four neighboring pixels with values $v_{11}, v_{12}, v_{21}, v_{22}$, then: $ V(x,y) = w_{11}v_{11} + w_{12}v_{12} + w_{21}v_{21} + w_{22}v_{22} $ where the weights $w_{ij}$ are proportional to the distance from $(x,y)$ to each pixel center. 4. Average the sampled values to get the bin output. Repeat for all bins. The result is a 2 × 2 feature map (or 7 × 7 in practice) that is perfectly aligned with the RoI, without quantization. #### PyTorch-style implementation PyTorch provides `roi_align` in `torchvision.ops`, which implements exactly this idea. ```python from torchvision.ops import roi_align # feature_map: [B, C, H, W] # rois: tensor of shape [num_rois, 5] where each row is [batch_idx, x1, y1, x2, y2] pooled = roi_align( feature_map, rois, output_size=(7, 7), # pooled to 7x7 spatial_scale=1/16, # if backbone stride = 16 sampling_ratio=2 # number of samples per bin ) ``` #### Why it matters For bounding box detection, the rounding error of RoI Pooling caused only small accuracy drops. But for masks, even a few pixels of misalignment ruin the output. RoI Align solved this issue, making instance segmentation practical for the first time. ### Step 4: Detection Head The detection head is very similar to Faster R-CNN. After RoI Align, each proposal is represented as a fixed feature map (for example 256 × 7 × 7). These features are flattened and fed into fully connected layers, which branch into classification and bounding box regression outputs. #### Implementation ```python class DetectionHead(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, num_classes, roi_size=7): super().__init__() # Flattened feature size = in_channels * roi_size * roi_size self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_channels * roi_size * roi_size, 1024) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(1024, 1024) # Classification branch: predicts class scores self.cls_score = nn.Linear(1024, num_classes + 1) # +1 for background # Regression branch: predicts box deltas self.bbox_pred = nn.Linear(1024, num_classes * 4) def forward(self, x): x = x.flatten(start_dim=1) x = nn.functional.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = nn.functional.relu(self.fc2(x)) cls_logits = self.cls_score(x) # [N, num_classes+1] bbox_deltas = self.bbox_pred(x) # [N, num_classes*4] return cls_logits, bbox_deltas ``` #### Example If we have 80 object categories (COCO dataset): - Classification outputs 81 scores per RoI (80 classes + background). - Regression outputs 320 values per RoI (80 classes × 4 deltas). ### Step 5: Mask Head The mask head is the unique addition in Mask R-CNN. Instead of fully connected layers, it uses convolutions to preserve spatial structure. It takes higher-resolution RoI features (14 × 14) and outputs a binary mask for each class at 28 × 28 resolution. #### Implementation ```python class MaskHead(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, num_classes, roi_size=14): super().__init__() # Four 3x3 convolutional layers layers = [] for _ in range(4): layers.append(nn.Conv2d(in_channels, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1)) layers.append(nn.ReLU(inplace=True)) self.convs = nn.Sequential(*layers) # Upsample with a transpose convolution self.deconv = nn.ConvTranspose2d(256, 256, kernel_size=2, stride=2) # Final 1x1 conv to output K masks of size 28x28 self.mask_pred = nn.Conv2d(256, num_classes, kernel_size=1) def forward(self, x): # Input: [N, C, 14, 14] after RoI Align x = self.convs(x) x = nn.functional.relu(self.deconv(x)) # [N, 256, 28, 28] masks = self.mask_pred(x) # [N, num_classes, 28, 28] return masks ``` #### Training - For each positive RoI, only the mask corresponding to its ground truth class is used in the loss. - The loss is a pixel-wise binary cross entropy across the 28 × 28 mask. - This avoids competition between classes and makes training more stable. Example If we detect a “person” in an RoI: - The detection head predicts class = “person”. - The mask head outputs 80 masks (one for each class in COCO). - We select only the “person” mask (28 × 28). - The mask is resized to the RoI’s bounding box and placed back into the image. ## Limitations Mask R-CNN was a huge leap forward, but it was not without trade-offs. The first limitation was **speed**. Even with the RPN and shared backbone, it remained a two-stage detector. Running RoI Align, a detection head, and a mask head for thousands of proposals made it too slow for real-time applications like robotics or live video. The second limitation was **computational cost**. The mask branch, with its extra convolutions, added significant memory and compute requirements. On large datasets like COCO, training Mask R-CNN required multiple GPUs and long training schedules. Deploying it on edge devices was not practical. The third limitation was **small object segmentation**. While the FPN improved small object detection, segmenting tiny objects remained a challenge. A 28 × 28 mask is already coarse, and when upsampled back to the original resolution, the fine details can get lost. Thin structures such as bicycle spokes or tree branches often came out blurry. Finally, like Faster R-CNN, it was still somewhat complex to train. The multi-task loss, balancing between RPN, classification, bounding box regression, and masks, required careful tuning. ## Reflections When I first studied Mask R-CNN, what impressed me was how *natural* the extension felt. The authors did not try to reinvent object detection. They simply took the successful Faster R-CNN framework and asked, “what if we add one more branch for masks.” This simplicity is what made it so powerful. By keeping the detection head unchanged and only adding the mask head, the model became modular, easy to extend, and still very accurate. The introduction of RoI Align was also an important lesson. Sometimes small design decisions, like whether to round coordinates or interpolate them, can make a massive difference. Bounding boxes were tolerant to the quantization error of RoI Pooling, but masks were not. RoI Align fixed this and made the whole model practical. For me, Mask R-CNN represents the point where deep learning in computer vision stopped being just about “detecting things” and started being about *understanding them in detail*. The ability to say not only “there is a person” but also “these are the exact pixels of the person” opened up fields like panoptic segmentation, DensePose, and keypoint detection. It showed how modular design lets us build more and more complex vision systems on top of the same foundations. My main takeaway is that progress in computer vision often comes from asking simple questions. Faster R-CNN solved region proposals, and Mask R-CNN asked: what if we also predict masks. That single step created one of the most widely used baselines in research and industry.

`,(0,n.jsxDEV)(e.p,{children:`By separating the mask prediction into its own branch, Mask R-CNN keeps the detection head focused
on classification and bounding box refinement, while the mask head specializes in pixel-level
segmentation. This parallel design is efficient because both branches share the same RoI features

upsampled later to the input resolution. Even at this size, it is accurate enough to capture fine
object boundaries.`},void 0,!1,{fileName:"C:\\Users\\gitan\\Workspace\\Personal_Projects\\webdev_projects\\new-personal-portfolio\\content\\blog\\_mdx_bundler_entry_point-3cd62731-7187-4682-ac90-6f8bb4c0445d.mdx",lineNumber:332,columnNumber:1},this),`
